faq.q: What is the most reliable cheap touring motorcycle?
faq.a: The Suzuki V-Strom 650 (2004-2020) is the most reliable budget tourer, with proven examples exceeding 100,000 miles on regular servicing alone. The Honda CBF600 runs a close second with typical Honda bulletproof reliability.

faq.q: How much should I budget for a cheap touring motorcycle?
faq.a: Expect to pay £1,500-£5,000 for the bike itself, plus £300-£600 for essential upgrades like luggage, heated grips, and an improved screen. Annual running costs including insurance, servicing, and tyres run £900-£1,600 for 6,000-8,000 miles.

faq.q: Can a cheap motorcycle handle long-distance UK touring?
faq.a: Absolutely. Japanese bikes like the V-Strom 650, CBF600, and Versys 650 are proven for multi-day tours across Scotland, Wales, and England. Reliability and comfort matter more than price—proper maintenance is key.

faq.q: What should I check when buying a used touring motorcycle?
faq.a: Service history is non-negotiable. Check tyres, chain condition, suspension function, and electrics thoroughly. Always test ride for at least 20 minutes covering different road types. Walk away if anything feels wrong.

faq.q: Are heated grips necessary for UK motorcycle touring?
faq.a: Heated grips are essential for extending your riding season in Britain. They cost £50-70 and make riding from October to March comfortable. They're the single best upgrade for British weather touring.

faq.q: What's better for budget touring: adventure bikes or road bikes?
faq.a: Both work brilliantly. Adventure-styled bikes like the V-Strom offer better weather protection and luggage capacity, while road bikes like the CBF600 are lighter and nimbler. Choose based on your typical routes and comfort preference.

Best Cheap Touring Motorcycles: Budget-Friendly Bikes for UK Adventures

Look, I get it. Not everyone can drop ten grand on a shiny BMW GS or a Triumph Trophy. But here's the truth I've learned after years of riding across Britain: you don't need to remortgage your house to experience proper touring. Some of the best tours I've done have been on bikes that cost less than a decent used car.

I've spent the last decade riding everything from the North Coast 500 to Welsh mountain passes on bikes ranging from budget warriors to premium tourers. And honestly? The bike that cost me £2,500 gave me just as many memorable miles as the one that cost four times that. The difference is knowing what to look for and what compromises you can actually live with.

In this guide, I'm sharing the bikes I'd genuinely recommend to a mate who wants to start touring without breaking the bank. These are machines I've either ridden myself or seen perform reliably in the hands of riders I trust. No theoretical nonsense—just real-world advice from someone who's been caught in Scottish rain on most of them.

What Makes a Good Budget Tourer?

Before we dive into specific models, let me share what I've learned matters most when you're shopping for a cheap touring bike. It's not about having every bell and whistle—it's about getting the fundamentals right.

First up: reliability. A bike that breaks down in the Highlands costs you more than just repair bills. It ruins your trip. I always prioritise proven Japanese reliability over European character when budget's tight. You can buy charisma later when you've got more cash.

Second: comfort over distance. I've ridden 400 miles in a day on a sports bike and could barely walk afterwards. Your budget tourer needs a riding position that doesn't have you stopping every hour to stretch. An upright posture, decent seat, and sensible footpeg position matter more than you think.

Third: parts availability and running costs. There's no point buying a £1,500 bike if a service costs £400 and parts take three weeks to arrive from Germany. Stick with bikes that every mechanic knows and every parts supplier stocks.

Weather protection matters too. British weather is reliably unreliable. A bike with even basic weather protection makes the difference between an epic adventure and a miserable slog through the rain on the A9.

My Top Budget Touring Motorcycles for 2026

Suzuki V-Strom 650 (2004-2020 Models)

I'll be honest—I'm biased here because a second-generation V-Strom carried me across Scotland more times than I can count. You can pick up earlier models for £2,000-£3,500, and the later ones for £3,500-£5,000. For that money, you're getting one of the most dependable touring bikes ever made.

The 650cc V-twin engine is bulletproof. I've known riders with over 100,000 miles on the clock with nothing more than regular servicing. It's smooth, torquey, and sips fuel like a sensible bike should. I regularly see 55-60 mpg on tour, which means fewer fuel stops and more time enjoying roads like the ones on the NC500 complete route.

The riding position is spot-on for all-day comfort. At 6'2", I've done back-to-back 300-mile days without major aches. The seat's not plush, but it's good enough. Chuck a sheepskin cover on there if you're planning serious distance.

Weather protection from the screen is decent, though I'd recommend an aftermarket screen if you're over six foot. Luggage options are endless—OEM panniers, Givi, SW-Motech, you name it. I ran Oxford soft panniers from SportsBikeShop for two years before upgrading to hard cases.

The only downside? They're not the prettiest bikes on the road. But when you're riding through Glen Coe at sunset, who cares what it looks like?

Honda CBF600 (2004-2013)

If the V-Strom is the sensible adventure choice, the CBF600 is the underrated road-focused option. You can find these for £1,500-£3,000 depending on mileage and condition. They're often overlooked, which is exactly why they're such good value.

The inline-four engine is typical Honda—smooth, reliable, and willing to rev when you fancy it. It's more road-oriented than the V-Strom but still perfectly capable of handling everything Britain throws at it. I've ridden one loaded up through the Brecon Beacons in February rain, and it didn't miss a beat.

Comfort is excellent for a naked bike. The upright riding position and wide bars make town riding easy, while motorway work doesn't feel like a battle against the wind. Yes, you'll want a taller screen for serious distance, but that's a £100 fix.

Running costs are negligible. Services are cheap, parts are everywhere, and fuel economy sits around 50-55 mpg in real-world touring conditions. The only thing I'd change is the suspension—it's a bit soft if you're regularly loaded with gear, but it's not a dealbreaker.

Kawasaki Versys 650 (2007-2014)

The Versys shares its engine with the ER-6, which means proven reliability and cheap parts. Early models go for £2,500-£4,000 now, making them cracking value for what you get.

I've borrowed a mate's 2010 Versys for a week-long tour through Scotland, and it surprised me. The parallel-twin engine has character—it's not as smooth as the Honda four-cylinder, but it's got more low-down grunt for overtakes on A-roads. Perfect for the kind of riding you do on routes like Island to Highlands.

The tall, upright seating position gives you a commanding view of the road. Some riders find it too tall, but at my height, I loved it. Shorter riders might struggle, so definitely sit on one before buying. The seat itself is firm but supportive over distance.

Handling is surprisingly nimble for an adventure-styled bike. It's lighter than the V-Strom and feels more playful on twisty B-roads. Weather protection is minimal on early models—budget for an aftermarket screen if you're doing serious miles.

The only quirk is the fueling can be slightly snatchy at low revs on earlier models. It's not a problem once you're used to it, but worth knowing before you test ride.

Yamaha Fazer 600 (1998-2003)

Old-school choice here, but hear me out. You can pick up a tidy Fazer 600 for £1,200-£2,000. Yes, they're getting on a bit, but the Thundercat engine is legendary for reliability. I know riders still touring on 25-year-old examples.

The fully-faired design gives proper weather protection—something you appreciate when the British summer delivers another week of rain. The riding position splits the difference between sports and touring, leaning slightly towards sporty. It's comfortable enough for 200-mile days but might leave you shifting around on longer hauls.

Performance is genuinely impressive for the price. The 600cc inline-four loves to rev and has enough punch to make overtaking safe and simple. Fuel economy hovers around 45-50 mpg depending on how much you twist the throttle.

The challenge with Fazers at this age is finding a well-maintained example. Service history is crucial—walk away from anything without it. Also check for corrosion, especially around the frame and exhaust. A thorough inspection is essential, but find a good one and you've got a brilliant budget tourer.

Triumph Tiger 955i (2001-2006)

Controversial pick because Triumphs aren't known for rock-bottom running costs, but the 955i Tigers are now cheap enough to consider. Expect to pay £2,000-£3,500 for a decent example.

The triple engine is what makes this bike special. It's got character that the Japanese bikes can't match—a distinctive sound and punchy delivery that makes every ride feel special. I've ridden one through the Yorkshire Dales and grinned the entire way.

Comfort is excellent with a plush seat and upright position. The screen offers good protection, and there's enough room for proper luggage. It feels like a bigger, more substantial bike than its Japanese rivals.

Here's the catch: reliability is good but not Honda-level bulletproof. The regulator/rectifier can fail (budget £150-200 for a replacement), and services are pricier than Japanese equivalents. Parts are still available but cost more. If you can live with slightly higher running costs for that British character, the 955i is brilliant. If you want absolute minimum expense, stick with Japanese.

What to Check Before Buying

I've made mistakes buying used bikes, so let me save you the pain. When you're looking at budget tourers, here's what actually matters:

  • Service history: Non-negotiable. A cheaper bike with full history beats a pristine-looking one with no paperwork every time.
  • Tyres: Check tread depth and age. Replacing both tyres adds £200-300 to your purchase price.
  • Chain and sprockets: A worn chain means immediate expense. Look for signs of maintenance—a clean, lubricated chain suggests a caring owner.
  • Suspension: Sit on the bike and bounce it. It should feel controlled, not bouncy or harsh. Fork seals shouldn't leak.
  • Electrics: Test everything—lights, indicators, horn, instruments. Electrical gremlins are frustrating and expensive to chase.
  • Corrosion: Inevitable on older bikes but check it's surface-level. Pitting on chrome and light rust are fine; structural corrosion isn't.
  • Test ride: Absolutely essential. The bike should pull smoothly, change gear cleanly, and brake straight. Any clunks, rattles, or weirdness need investigating.

Don't rush this process. I've driven three hours to view a bike only to walk away after ten minutes because something didn't feel right. That's fine—better than buying someone else's problem.

Essential Upgrades for Budget Touring

Even the best budget tourer needs a few additions to make it properly tour-ready. Here's what I always budget for after buying:

Luggage

You need somewhere to put your stuff. Hard panniers are ideal but expensive—budget £300-600 for decent cases. Soft luggage is cheaper (£100-200) and perfectly adequate for most touring. I've used both extensively. Soft luggage is fine until you want to leave the bike and walk around a town without worrying about someone slashing your bags.

Don't forget a tank bag. They're brilliant for maps, phone, wallet, and snacks. Magnetic ones are easiest, but make sure they fit your tank shape. Budget £40-80.

Screen

Most budget bikes have inadequate screens for serious touring. An aftermarket screen transforms motorway riding. Expect to pay £80-150. The difference on a 200-mile motorway slog is huge—less buffeting means less fatigue.

Heated Grips

Game-changer for British touring. I've ridden from October to March thanks to heated grips. Oxford heated grips cost around £50-70 and install easily. They're worth every penny when you're riding through the Highlands in April and it's somehow still freezing.

Phone Mount and USB Socket

Modern touring needs navigation. A decent phone mount (£30-50) and USB socket (£15-25) turn your phone into a satnav. Use our route building tool to plan your rides, then follow them on your phone. Make sure you get a weatherproof USB socket—I've fried two phones by using cheap ones in the rain.

The best touring bike is the one you can afford to run reliably. A £3,000 bike you can maintain properly beats a £6,000 bike you can't afford to service.

Running Costs Reality Check

Let me give you real numbers from my experience running budget tourers. These are approximate annual costs assuming you do around 6,000-8,000 miles per year:

  • Insurance: £200-500 depending on age, location, and experience. Shop around every year.
  • Servicing: £200-400 if you DIY basic services, £400-700 if you use a garage for everything. Japanese bikes sit at the lower end.
  • Tyres: £250-350 per year if you're doing proper mileage. Budget brands are fine—I've used Michelin Road 5s and cheaper options with similar results.
  • Chain/sprockets: £150-200 every 15,000-20,000 miles if you maintain them properly.
  • Consumables: Oil, filters, brake pads, coolant—budget £100-150 annually.

Total: roughly £900-1,600 per year excluding fuel. That's manageable on most budgets and works out at £75-130 per month. Add fuel on top—figure £30-50 for a typical weekend tour depending on how far you ride.

Where Budget Bikes Excel

Here's something people don't talk about enough: cheap bikes make you a better, more confident rider. When you're not worried about dropping a £12,000 GS in a gravel car park, you relax and enjoy yourself more.

I've ridden budget bikes down rough forest tracks I'd never attempt on an expensive machine. I've parked them in dodgy areas without losing sleep. I've learned to do my own maintenance because I couldn't afford not to, which made me more self-sufficient on tour.

Budget bikes also let you spend money on the stuff that actually matters—better gear, more fuel, extra nights away, proper waterproofs. I'd rather ride a £2,500 bike wearing £500 of quality kit than a £6,000 bike in cheap gear. The bike doesn't keep you dry and warm; your jacket does.

For exploring Britain's best roads, you don't need massive horsepower or electronic suspension. You need reliability, comfort, and enough character to make the journey enjoyable. Every bike I've recommended delivers that. Check out our packing checklist to make sure you're properly prepared for your first tour.

British Weather Considerations

Let's be real about UK touring: you will get wet. I've been soaked in June and frozen in September. Your budget tourer needs to handle this reality.

All the bikes I've recommended cope fine with wet roads—modern tyres are excellent in the rain. What matters more is keeping you comfortable. A bike with decent weather protection, heated grips, and space for proper waterproof luggage makes British weather manageable rather than miserable.

I've learned to embrace it. Some of my best rides have been in drizzle through the Scottish Borders or fighting crosswinds on the North York Moors. The key is having gear that works and a bike you trust. When you're not worried about whether the engine will start after sitting in the rain, you can focus on enjoying the ride.

Take Action and Start Touring

Right, that's enough theory. Here's what you actually need to do: set a realistic budget including running costs and upgrades. Browse classified ads but don't rush. When you find something promising, inspect it thoroughly or pay a mechanic to do it for you. Test ride it properly—at least 20 minutes including motorway, town, and twisty roads if possible.

Once you've bought your budget tourer, spend your first few rides getting comfortable with it loaded. Do a practice run close to home before attempting a week-long tour. Learn basic maintenance—chain adjustment, oil changes, basic checks. It saves money and makes you more confident on the road.

Then just go ride. Use our trip planning tool to map out your first proper tour. Start with a weekend away, then build up to longer trips as your confidence grows. The best memories I've made on two wheels have been on bikes that cost less than some people spend on a holiday.

Britain has incredible roads waiting for you. You don't need an expensive bike to explore them—you just need to get out there and ride.
